passages.where: A hymn of wonder at God who feeds every creature, from wild donkeys to lions. Among the gifts he brings from the earth are bread that sustains, oil that makes the face shine, and wine that gladdens the heart. Wine, olive oil and bread were the three great crops of the land, and the psalm counts all three as God's kindness.

The chapter opens by personifying wine and strong drink as a mocker and a brawler. The danger is not only in the bottle but in being led astray by it. Whoever is ruled by drink, the proverb says, is not wise.

A father pleads with his son to keep his heart on the right path and not to join those who drink too much or gorge themselves. Proverbs names the cost in plain terms: poverty, and a drowsiness that leaves a person in rags.

In a series of woes against Judah, Isaiah describes people who rise early to chase strong drink and stay up late inflamed by wine, with music at their feasts. Their problem, he says, is that they do not regard the work of the LORD. Drinking has become a way of not paying attention to God.

The first story after God's covenant with Noah is a failure. Noah, the righteous man who came through the flood, plants a vineyard, becomes drunk and lies exposed in his tent. Two of his sons cover him without looking. Scripture tells of the good man's fall plainly and without mockery.

Paul was writing into a city where drinking parties and the worship of Dionysus, the god of wine, were part of public life. He sets two kinds of filling side by side: drunkenness, which leads to reckless excess, and being filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing, thanksgiving and mutual submission.

Paul is settling a quarrel in Rome between believers who ate and drank freely and believers who abstained. He tells neither side to despise the other, and tells the stronger to give up a freedom rather than cause a brother or sister to stumble. Love for the other person outranks one's own liberty.

In the middle of instructions about elders, Paul gives Timothy a personal word: stop drinking only water and use a little wine for your stomach and frequent illnesses. Ancient medicine used wine for digestive ailments. Timothy seems to have been abstaining, and Paul tells him to take a little for his health.

Jesus describes his critics' inconsistency: John the Baptist fasted and they called him demon-possessed; the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and a drunkard. The slander was false, but it shows that Jesus ate and drank at ordinary tables with ordinary people.

God has Jeremiah set wine before the Rechabites, a family who had kept their ancestor's command for generations never to drink wine. They refuse, and God holds up their faithfulness as a rebuke to Judah, which would not obey its God. Scripture honors their abstaining as faithfulness.

Paul closes a long discussion of food and drink offered in a pagan city with one rule for everything: whether you eat or drink, do it all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

misread.taken: The wedding at Cana is used in two opposite ways: by some to show that drinking is always fine because Jesus made wine, and by others to argue that what Jesus made must have been unfermented juice, so that the Bible approves only of abstaining.
misread.says: Neither reading fits the story well. Most scholars think the word for wine and the master of the banquet's remark mean real wine, which was the normal drink of a feast and was usually mixed with water. On the other side, the story gives no approval to drunkenness, which Scripture condemns. The miracle saves a family from shame at a village wedding, and John calls it the first sign of Jesus' glory. It is about Jesus bringing the joy God had promised, not about drinking, and the joy it shows is in him, not in a cup.

whole: For some people alcohol is a glass of wine with dinner; for others it is the thing that wrecked their childhood home, or the thing they are quietly drinking more of each year. Christians disagree about it, sometimes sharply, and many carry the questions privately: whether it is wrong to drink at all, whether their own drinking has become a problem, or how to live with someone whose drinking frightens them.

The Bible holds two truths about wine together, and does not let either swallow the other. Wine is a gift: the psalm counts it among God's kindnesses, Jesus' first sign is wine at a wedding, and Paul tells Timothy to drink a little for his health. Drunkenness is a sin: Proverbs calls wine a mocker, Isaiah pronounces woe on those who chase strong drink, Noah's story shows a good man undone, and Paul sets drunkenness against being filled with the Spirit. Scripture never calls wine evil in itself, and it never treats drunkenness lightly. It also honors those who abstain, as God did the Rechabites.

Underneath the question of drinking is usually a question of what is ruling us. Proverbs says the problem is being led astray. Isaiah's drinkers had stopped paying attention to God. Paul's contrast is between two kinds of filling. Alcohol is often reached for to quiet anxiety, numb grief, or fill an emptiness, and when it becomes the way a person gets through, it has started to rule. That is true whether someone drinks a lot or a little.

So the wisdom here is honesty before rules. Ask what drinking is doing for you, and whether you could stop for a month without strain; if you could not, take that seriously and tell someone. If drinking has hurt your family, you do not owe anyone a drink, and your caution is wisdom, not weakness. If you drink with freedom, use it with love, as Romans 14 asks, and never press a drink on someone whose story you do not know. And whether you drink or abstain, do it to the glory of God, without despising the brother or sister who chooses differently.

differ.share: Christians agree that drunkenness is sin, that no one should be pressured to drink, that those harmed by alcohol and those caught in it need care, and that believers should not despise one another over a matter Scripture leaves to conscience (Romans 14).

views.name: Abstinence
views.body: Many Baptist, Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal churches have long taught or encouraged abstaining from alcohol altogether. They point to its power to harm and enslave, the warnings of Proverbs, the example of the Rechabites, and the call in Romans 14 to give up a freedom for the sake of others.

views.name: Moderation
views.body: Many other Christians, among them Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed churches, hold that drinking in moderation is a lawful use of God's gift. They point to Psalm 104, the wedding at Cana and wine at the Lord's Supper, while warning just as seriously against drunkenness.

differ.after: Both take the danger seriously and both honor the gift of a clear mind. The test Paul gives fits both: whether you eat or drink, do it all to the glory of God.

sit: What does drinking do for you that you have not told anyone, and is there something it is helping you avoid?

prayer.lead: Psalm 104 counts wine among God's gifts and ends by turning to the giver. Pray these lines from its close as a way of keeping every gift in its place.

Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you.
